kur1: What causes pain between the shoulder blades, and when is it dangerous? Warning signs that help tell it apart from pain coming from the neck or the heart, what helps, and six exercises to do at home.
kur2: Pain between the shoulder blades (upper back pain)
kur3: An ache, burning or sharp pain between the shoulder blades or in the middle of the back is very common. The thoracic spine is strong, and most people get better with simple measures and regular movement. Even so, pain can be referred to this area from the neck and, rarely, from internal organs such as the heart, so it is important to know which symptoms should not wait.

kur35: Can pain between my shoulder blades come from the heart?
kur36: Rarely, yes. In a heart attack, the pain is usually a tightness or pressure in the chest; it can spread to the arm, neck and jaw, and may come with breathlessness, sweating and nausea. Sudden, very severe chest or back pain that feels like tearing can be a sign of a tear in the main artery (aortic dissection). With these symptoms, call 112 without waiting. Pain that changes with movement and position more often comes from muscles and joints, but this alone does not rule out the heart.
kur37: Can the pain come from the neck?
kur38: Yes. When a nerve root in the neck is compressed, pain around the shoulder blade is common and can sometimes start weeks before arm pain. If you have pain spreading to the arm, numbness or weakness, you can look at the cervical disc herniation guide and see a doctor or physiotherapist.
kur39: The thoracic spine is a strong structure, and most people get better with simple measures. Symptoms can last a few weeks, sometimes a few months. Keeping active and doing the exercises regularly supports recovery.
kur40: My child’s back hurts; is it the school bag?
kur41: It may be, but it may not be the only cause. Studies have reported back pain more often in children and adolescents, especially girls, than in adults, and backpack use is one of the factors linked with it. Factors such as stress, sleep and activity habits are worth looking at too. If the pain does not settle or there are warning signs, you can have your child seen by a doctor.
